title: Scope and Lifetime of Local Variables
learningObjectives: Define scope and distinguish it from lifetime.
Identify the block in which a local variable can be accessed.
Explain the scope of a for-loop iteration variable.
Recognize that separate method calls have separate local variables.
Use nested blocks and methods to organize temporary values safely.

understand.concept: Scope determines where a variable name can be used in source code. A local variable is generally scoped to the block in which it is declared, including the method or nested block. Lifetime describes how long the variable's storage is relevant during execution; it is not identical to lexical scope.
understand.whyItMatters: Understanding scope prevents accidental name conflicts and helps keep temporary data close to the code that uses it. It also makes methods easier to reason about and test.
understand.analogy: Scope is like the area of a building where a keycard grants access. Lifetime is how long the keycard remains active. The two ideas are related but not identical.
understand.analogyLimit: C# compiler rules determine lexical visibility, while runtime implementation details determine storage and lifetime. Captured locals in lambdas or local functions can outlive the method activation in which they were created.

explain.narrative:
## Block scope

A local declared inside a block is visible only within that block and its nested blocks, subject to C# declaration-space rules. It cannot be referenced after the closing brace.

## Method scope

Each method invocation has its own local variables and parameters. A local in one method is not directly visible in another method; pass values as parameters or return results when data must cross method boundaries.

## Loop variables

A variable declared in a for initializer is scoped to the loop statement. It is not available after the loop. A foreach iteration variable is similarly scoped to its foreach statement.

## Scope versus lifetime

Scope is a compile-time language concept describing where a name can be referenced. Lifetime is a runtime concept describing how long a variable's storage remains relevant. Captured locals in lambdas or local functions can outlive the method activation in which they were created.

## Version baseline

These scope rules are long-standing C# behaviour and apply to C# 14 and .NET 10.

examples.title: A for-loop variable
examples.explanation: index is declared in the for statement and is not used after the loop.

examples.title: Nested block scope
examples.explanation: The nested block can read total from its enclosing scope, but extra is local to the nested block.

examples.title: Independent method calls
examples.explanation: Each call creates its own local value. Updating it in one invocation does not change the next invocation's local.
